title: Excited, Skeptical, or Worried? A Multi-Institutional Study of Student Views on Generative AI in Computing Education
venue: Proceedings of the 25th Koli Calling International Conference on Computing Education Research
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how students in different educational contexts use and perceive generative AI (GenAI) in computing education. The central research question is how students from high schools, vocational colleges, and research universities differ in their GenAI usage patterns, attitudes, ethical views, and perceptions of institutional policy. The study addresses a gap in prior research, which has largely focused on university students and has provided less insight into high school and vocational college settings.

The authors conducted a multi-institutional survey in the Netherlands, adapting prior survey instruments on GenAI in computing education. The final survey included both closed-ended items and open-ended questions, allowing the researchers to analyze quantitative patterns as well as qualitative student rationales. The study collected 410 responses from students enrolled in computing-related programs across 23 institutions: 7 high schools, 7 colleges offering vocational computing programs, and 9 research universities. Participants included high school students in final years of secondary education and higher education students in Bachelor’s and Master’s programs. The survey examined GenAI use for tasks such as learning, text work, programming, debugging, help-seeking, and assignment support, along with attitudes, ethics, and perceived course-level effects.

The findings show clear differences by institution type. High school students used GenAI more for text-related tasks and concept learning, while college students reported the highest programming-related use, and university students also used GenAI frequently for coding and debugging. Across all groups, students commonly reported excitement, optimism, and gratitude toward GenAI, but higher education students expressed more skepticism, stress, and worry, whereas high school students showed more trust and fewer negative emotions. Most students across contexts believed GenAI should be allowed under certain conditions, especially to support learning but not for exams or graded work. High school and college students also held more permissive ethical views about GenAI-assisted assignment completion than university students.

Overall, the paper concludes that students’ perceptions and uses of GenAI differ meaningfully across educational levels and institutional types, likely reflecting differences in educational goals, exposure, and policy environments. The authors argue that these differences have implications for GenAI literacy, policy communication, and instructional design, especially for supporting students transitioning from high school into higher education. They also note that GenAI had little influence on high school students’ decision to pursue computing studies.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generative AI tools and large language model chatbots used broadly for text generation, code generation, explanations, and learning support, without a single focal product evaluated as the intervention.
identified_tools.use_case: Surveyed computing students across high school, vocational college, and research university about how they use and perceive generative AI tools in computing education, including programming, text work, learning support, help-seeking, ethics, and attitudes.

findings.finding_summary: Across 410 students from 23 Dutch institutions, usage patterns differed by educational level. High school students used GenAI mainly for text tasks and learning about topics and concepts, while college students reported the most frequent programming-related use; all groups reported similarly frequent use for learning, with no significant group difference, H(2)=4.16, p=.125.
findings.measure: Self-reported GenAI use frequency across tasks (text work, learning, code generation, debugging, programming-related tasks)

findings.finding_summary: High school students were less likely than college and university students to agree that frequent GenAI use for code generation hinders learning. Significant pairwise differences were reported for high school vs. college (U=7060, p_adj=.025) and high school vs. university (U=3936, p_adj=.002); among higher education students, more frequent programming-related GenAI use was negatively associated with concern that it hinders learning.
findings.measure: Agreement that frequent GenAI use for code generation hinders ability to learn programming
findings.effect_size: U=7060; U=3936; correlations reported as weak to moderate negative associations

findings.finding_summary: Students showed mixed views on whether GenAI can guide as effectively as human teachers. High school students agreed more often than higher education students, with a significant difference between high school and university students (U=10354, p_adj=.031); in higher education, more frequent GenAI use was positively associated with agreement that GenAI provides effective guidance.
findings.measure: Agreement that GenAI provides guidance as effectively as human teachers
findings.effect_size: U=10354; correlations reported as weak to strong positive associations

findings.finding_summary: Across all groups, students expressed excitement, optimism, and gratitude toward GenAI, while fear was less common. Higher education students more often reported worry and skepticism, whereas high school students reported greater trust and fewer negative feelings; for example, worry differed significantly for high school vs. college (U=7073, p_adj=.026) and high school vs. university (U=3677, p_adj<.001).
findings.measure: Self-reported attitudes and emotions toward GenAI, including trust, excitement, optimism, worry, skepticism, stress, gratitude, and fright

findings.finding_summary: Higher GenAI usage was associated with more positive attitudes and fewer negative attitudes in higher education. For college and university students, the paper reports moderate negative associations between usage and skepticism/worry, and moderate to strong positive associations between usage and optimism, excitement, and gratitude; among high school students, text-related GenAI use was positively associated with excitement (r_s=.449, p<.001).
findings.measure: Spearman correlations between GenAI use frequency and emotional attitudes toward GenAI
findings.effect_size: r_s=.449 for high school text use and excitement; other correlations described as weak to strong/moderate to strong

findings.finding_summary: Students across educational types generally believed GenAI should be allowed to support learning under conditions, but not for exams or graded assignments. College students reported more permissive institutional policies than high school and university students, with significant differences for high school vs. college (chi-square(3)=24.38, p_adj<.001) and college vs. university (chi-square(3)=18.91, p_adj<.001).
findings.measure: Perceived institutional GenAI policy clarity and allowance spectrum; student views on whether GenAI should be allowed
findings.sample_size: n=384 for open-response permissibility item; n=410 overall survey

findings.finding_summary: High school students reported higher perceived misuse of GenAI by themselves and their peers than higher education students. Significant differences were found for perceived peer misuse (high school vs. college U=11065, p_adj<.001; high school vs. university U=6426.5, p_adj=.006) and for self-reported personal misuse (high school vs. college U=12344, p_adj<.001; high school vs. university U=6670.5, p_adj<.001).
findings.measure: Perceived peer misuse of GenAI and self-reported use of GenAI when not allowed

findings.finding_summary: High school and college students held more permissive ethical views than university students on using GenAI for assignments. The share considering it ethical to auto-generate an entire assignment and submit it after understanding it was 34.9% in high school, 26.1% in college, and 8.3% in university; significant differences were high school vs. university (chi-square(1)=21.17, p_adj<.001) and college vs. university (chi-square(1)=14.29, p_adj<.001).
findings.measure: Ethical judgments about auto-generating full or partial assignments with GenAI

findings.finding_summary: Within course-specific responses, most students reported that GenAI enhanced rather than hindered their learning process, helping with examples, summaries, explanations, debugging, and coding speed. Some students also reported that GenAI hindered learning by reducing the need to think independently; these are qualitative self-reports rather than measured learning gains.
findings.measure: Open-ended self-reported perceived effect of GenAI on course learning process

findings.finding_summary: Students commonly reported using GenAI because it makes work easier or faster, and many perceived it as accelerating their learning in courses. College students were the largest group to agree that GenAI played a large role in their learning process (47.9%) and accelerated their learning (55.1%), though the paper states these differences were not statistically significant among groups.
findings.measure: Self-reported reasons for using GenAI in course work and agreement that GenAI accelerated learning
findings.sample_size: course-specific respondents n=356 overall, with most completing both survey parts

findings.finding_summary: The rise of GenAI had minimal influence on high school students' decision to pursue computing. Among 80 high school students answering this item, 79% reported no influence, while similarly small shares reported positive (11%) or negative (10%) influence.
findings.measure: Self-reported influence of GenAI on high school students' study-choice intentions toward computing

quality_tier_rationale: This is an exploratory multi-institutional survey with quantitative and qualitative analyses, using non-parametric tests and correlations, but it is observational and based on self-report rather than causal evaluation of an intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports meaningful differences in perceptions, usage, and attitudes, but no direct causal learning effect sizes or objective achievement impacts. Effects are primarily descriptive, correlational, and often mixed or context-dependent.
